title: The paper your AI never saw
subtitle: Five real citations. One invisible problem.
author: Aaron Tay

scenes.title: Five real citations. What is missing?
A missing citation is a mystery
What you typed is not what you need

lines.text: Here are five papers. Every citation is real. Every summary is accurate. Would you trust the answer?
Now I put a sixth paper on the table. It is the landmark study everyone in the field would name. Your answer never mentioned it.
Nothing was fabricated. And yet the evidence is incomplete. The interesting question is not just what the AI wrote. It is what the AI ever got to see.
Let's try a thought experiment. These cards represent an index. A search sends thirty of them to a second machine. We will call those the candidates.
That machine can inspect the cards carefully, change their order, and choose five for a writer. Watch the numbered cards move. They are still the same thirty.
But the gold card, our landmark paper, stayed behind. Can a better reranker rescue it?
No. Reordering thirty cards cannot introduce a thirty first. Another retrieval round could bring it in. More fluent writing cannot establish evidence from a source the writer was never given.
This is more than a card trick. Chapter one describes Primo Research Assistant, using documentation checked in September twenty twenty six.
A language model converts the question into Boolean variations connected by OR. That query searches the Central Discovery Index and returns up to thirty results.
Embeddings rerank those candidates to select five sources. Only then does a language model write an overview from their abstracts.
There are two jobs here. Retrieval selects the evidence. Generation writes the answer. Notice that a language model can help with either job. Its presence does not identify the retrieval method.
So did retrieval fail when our landmark paper vanished? Not necessarily. A missing citation is a mystery, not a diagnosis.
Maybe the index did not cover it. Maybe the query missed it. Maybe it lost at the thirty candidate boundary, or when thirty became five.
Or it reached the writer, and the writer left it out. Inspect the supplied working set first. A direct search for that paper tests availability. It cannot reconstruct where the original run lost it.
There is an even earlier gap. You type three words: AI academic libraries. What does the machine know about what you actually want?
You want empirical studies since twenty twenty four, about academic libraries implementing generative AI services for research support.
The query is one imperfect expression of that purpose. The system observes a representation, not your full need.
Consider this record. It contains AI, academic, and libraries. Perfect word overlap. But it is an opinion piece from twenty nineteen.
Now consider an implementation study about large language models, research consultation, and a university library. It misses every exact query word, yet it may meet the need.
Watch the two sets. Matching the query and helping the reader overlap, but neither contains the other.
Boolean conditions, ranking scores, and embedding similarity provide evidence about relevance. They are not the reader's judgement.
Relevant can mean a computed match, topical suitability, what someone learns, or usefulness for a task.
These are different perspectives, not a ladder. The same paper can help a beginner understand a topic and fail a systematic review's inclusion rules.
Relevance is a relationship. Relevant to someone, for something.
Chapter one leaves us with three puzzles. First, add an invented word to a real question. If strict AND requires that word, the result set should be empty.
Yet the chapter's scite example still returns useful looking papers. Does that prove semantic retrieval? No. It challenges our assumption about the admission rule.
Keep the internal mechanism open. A screen shows behaviour, not a complete architecture.
Second, the chapter's Google Scholar search reports about nine point four million results, while only a thousand are viewable.
Animate those quantities separately. The reported count is enormous. The visible window is tiny.
The count alone does not tell us that every record was individually scored or ranked. How was the viewable fraction chosen?
Third, in the chapter's August twenty twenty six Semantic Scholar observation, the full question returns thirteen results.
Remove the extra question words, and the shorter keyword query returns about thirty five thousand three hundred. Same need. Very different result counts.
A name containing semantic does not establish a retrieval architecture. These observations are prompts to investigate, not proof of a hidden mechanism.
Zoom out. A useful map has six possible stages: query transformation, analysis and execution rules, first stage retrieval, fusion, reranking, and presentation.
Fusion combines candidate lists, perhaps from different queries or retrieval methods. Not every product uses every stage.
A controller chooses and sequences the actions. The shape of an answer does not reveal who chose the next search.
Separate two properties. Across this axis, the output changes from ranked records to a written answer.
Up this axis, retrieval changes from a single pass to repeated searches. That gives us quick search, quick answer, iterative search, and deep research.
Neither axis measures agency. A fixed workflow and an agent can occupy the same box.
So when an answer arrives, follow the evidence backwards. What was supplied? What was selected? What was searched?
That is the retrieval problem. Chapter two begins with the clearest admission rule of all: words as Boolean conditions.
